The night of the mikveh is an intimate one, best kept the secret of the husband and wife. The
only person privy to this knowledge is the ‘Mikveh-lady.’
Furthermore, the wife must immerse under the supervision of the ‘Mikveh-lady.’ Immersion,

Additionally, the fact that other women are present often adds to the wife’s concern that no

In light of the above, the role of the ‘Mikveh-lady’ assumes an added dimension. More than

Although each woman is different, the following points are offered as food for thought.
Sensitivity to the Woman Being Assisted
The ‘Mikveh-lady’ should be sensitive to the woman she is assisting. A bride preparing for
her wedding, for example, requires extra sensitivity. Often she approaches this night with
apprehension. In many instances her mother escorts her this first night to the mikveh. In such
cases the mother will wait in the waiting room or outside. Other women in the vicinity may
know the mother and be able to deduce that this evening her daughter is immersing. This may,
in certain cases add unnecessary distress to the daughter. Therefore, a little planning is in
order. Perhaps the arrangements may be made ahead of time for the bride to come later at
night when things have quieted. Or, a place for the mother to wait can be organized.
The ‘Mikveh-lady’ should be made aware any time a woman is being brought to the mikveh
for the first time or is new to the experience. This will allow her the opportunity to act
appropriately with added support and consideration.
Women have their emotional needs. Some women prefer the ‘Mikveh-lady’ to act casually;
not to make a fuss of her; not to raise her voice, calling attention. Some women like the
In general, the atmosphere created in the mikveh should be congenial and conducive to
In each mikveh different arrangements are in place. Some women dislike mikvehs where
the waiting room is communal. They dislike having to wait in sight of other women
mikvehs have sufficient space to alleviate this. Each ‘Mikveh-lady’ and communal Rabbi should
When the women have finished preparing themselves, they shouldn’t be kept waiting
unnecessarily. They should not be rushed to finish, on the one hand, yet when they have
concluded hafifah, effort should be made not to keep them waiting unnecessarily to immerse.
The water in the mikveh should be kept at as comfortable a temperature as possible. The
water shouldn’t be too hot nor too cold. The ‘Mikveh-lady’ should try to keep the material
necessary for the hafifah in stock and in place. This means that there should be enough soap,
nail cutters, towels, combs, etc. in the bathrooms, so that the women don’t have to request them.
Those responsible should make sure that there is sufficient light in the bathrooms for the
women to properly perform their hafifah.
Another point which can cause unnecessary stress to women is when those in charge of the
mikveh announce that the mikveh is closed at a certain hour and everyone should hurry. Of
course, the ‘Mikveh-lady’ works long hours, but arrangements should be made in the
community to allow for situations wherein a woman comes late to the mikveh and requires
time after the scheduled hours. If this necessitates the ‘Mikveh-lady’ to receive financial
compensation, this should be weighed positively by those responsible.
Remember, this is a special, intimate, and sensitive night for many women. Family life
revolving around immersion in the mikveh is the single most important ingredient in the
strength of every family and the entire Jewish nation. Every community must do its best to
ensure the ultimate comfort and convenience for this night, even if this involves added
financial outlay. No money could be better spent.
Experience shows that many women are tense about immersing in the mikveh. For some,
this is based on fear of submerging. This may be accented by time pressure or fear of being
observed. For others, this might be based on anxiety about performing the mitzvah properly.
Regardless of the reason, this is counterproductive. You should condition yourself mentally
that no one is watching with a stopwatch and if submerging is distressing, you can go about it
slowly. In fact, you should go into immersion happily. This night is the culmination of at least
twelve days of separation from your husband and makes your intimate reunion possible. This
is the single most important act in the Jewish family and should be done with joyous
In most communities there are fixed times when the mikveh is open and the ‘Mikveh-lady’
receives a fixed salary or stipend. In places where a “tip” is the norm this should be taken
seriously, bearing in mind the important function the ‘Mikveh-lady’ fulfills, as well as the late
Only immersion in a kosher mikveh under constant supervision by an orthodox
rabbinical board, an orthodox Rabbi or G-d fearing person specifically trained to supervise its
upkeep, is able to remove the wife’s niddah state. Baths, swimming pools, Jacuzzis and the like
have no validity whatsoever in this context.
